quick.summary: Why unique tracking identifiers break your charts, and how to split the deep details out.
quick.takeaway: Put simple numbers into metrics. Keep the long, unique stories inside your logs.

parts.title: Too many labels

beats.line: Our dashboard froze when I looked up bad web requests.
Why does our own tracking tool crash when we need it?
Because you attached a unique user identifier to every single request.
Think of a library sorting books. Fiction or facts is easy.
Sure, that is just two big buckets.
But sorting by every exact minute a book was returned breaks the system.
It creates high cardinality dimensions.
Can I just call it too many unique labels?
I love it. Millions of unique labels make the dashboard choke.
But I need to know which users had failing requests?

parts.cliff: Where should those unique details go instead?

beats.line: So if unique labels break the charts, how do I find broken requests?
You separate the big trends from the deep details.
Think of a doctor. Heart rate and blood pressure use a chart.
Because those are just numbers going up or down.
Yes. In our system, those are your metrics. Keep them simple.
Then where do the long stories go? The exact user details?
The doctor writes those in their private notes.
For us, those exact details go into the written logs.
Oh. Use metrics to see the spike, and logs to read the details.
Exactly. Let each tool do what it does best.

quiz.question: Why does attaching a unique user identifier to every metric break the dashboard?
options: It creates too many unique labels for the system to group.
The identifiers take up too much physical space on the server.
It violates privacy laws to store identifiers.
Users can change their identifiers unexpectedly.
quiz.explanation: Metrics systems group items into buckets. Millions of unique labels mean millions of buckets, which overloads the system.

quiz.question: The best place to record deep, individual user details is in your metrics.
quiz.explanation: Metrics are for simple numbers and trends. Deep, exact details belong in your logs.
